ch02.note: The end of 1581. Chapter 1 opened in the spring of Tenshō 10 (1582); the narrator has now, as he promised there, turned the clock back about a year to rejoin Goemon. The whole of this chapter therefore runs up to, and through, the events of the first chapter from the other side.

Chinu (Chinu no umi) is the old poetic name for the stretch of sea off Sakai and Izumi, the eastern reach of what is now Osaka Bay. It is named again and again in the ancient poetry, which is the point of the lines that follow.

ch02.anchor: this poem stands in the Man'yōshū
ch02.note: The Man’yōshū (“Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves,” compiled in the eighth century) is Japan’s oldest anthology of verse. The poem — a lover soaked to the sleeve gathering shells on the Chinu shore — is one of its anonymous pieces; the narrator’s joke is that an unlettered thief like Goemon repeats its very gesture without any notion that a classical poem has said it first.

Nabari lies in the north of Iga province. The cover story is quietly ironic: to hide that he is an Iga shinobi, Goemon invents a false self who is nonetheless from Iga, planting “Tahei” a short ride from his real birthplace at Ishikawa.

The Ten Commandments as the Jesuits taught them in Japan; the “rules for the wiping-out of sin” are the examination of conscience made before confession. The numbering follows the Catholic decalogue — the sixth against adultery, the ninth against coveting another man’s wife — and the searching questions about sins of desire are drawn straight from the confessors’ manuals of the mission.

Nanzen-ji is a great Zen monastery in eastern Kyoto; its towering two-storey gate (the Sanmon) is bound up with the Goemon legend. In the famous kabuki Sanmon Gosan no Kiri (1778) the outlaw Goemon lounges atop this very gate and cries, at the spring view, “What a prospect! What a prospect!” The novel nods to that legend by lodging its Goemon in the gate-tower among the temple’s dry-lacquer Buddhas.

Kariteimo (Sanskrit Hārītī), popularly Kishimojin. By the legend she was an ogress who devoured other people’s children until the Buddha hid one of her own thousand children to teach her a mother’s grief; converted, she became the guardian of childbirth and of infants, and is shown holding a pomegranate. She is especially honored in Nichiren Buddhism.

ch02.anchor: a Santa Maria holding the child Jezus Kirishito
ch02.note: A Christian image made in Buddhist form. The Christian daimyō Takayama Ukon (see chapter 1) held Takatsuki from 1573 and raised churches there; a Madonna-and-Child carved by a Japanese Buddhist sculptor would sit at the very root of the later “Maria Kannon,” the disguised Marian images by which hidden Christians kept their faith through the persecution. Goemon, taking it for a Kishimojin, sees only that its face is Maki’s.

One of the most famous of the Sakai merchant princes, better remembered as Ruson (Luzon) Sukezaemon. As the text goes on to say, he sailed to Luzon in the Spanish Philippines and came home laden with treasure; he later fell foul of Hideyoshi, who coveted his imported wares, and by tradition fled Japan for the southern seas. Much of his story is half legend.

ch02.anchor: the History of the Western Religion in Japan
ch02.note: Nihon Seikyō-shi, a later Japanese history of the Christian mission drawing on the Jesuit letters and chronicles. Here it and Padre Gaspar Vilela’s 1562 letter (Vilela: see chapter 1) are cited as real documentary evidence for how strongly Sakai was fortified.

Sakai governed itself, in this age, through a council of thirty-six wealthy townsmen, the egōshū, the ten strongest of whom (the naya-shū, the “warehouse men”) held the real power. The Jesuit Frois likened the free merchant city to Venice. That autonomy ended when Nobunaga brought Sakai under a magistrate of his own.

ch02.anchor: Kuki Yoshitaka built ten iron ships
ch02.note: Kuki Yoshitaka was Nobunaga’s admiral. In 1578 he built a squadron of great iron-plated warships and with them smashed the Mōri navy at the mouth of the Kizu River, cutting off the sea route by which the Mōri had been resupplying the Ishiyama Hongan-ji. Most accounts number the ironclads at six or seven rather than the ten the novel gives.

The sotetsu (sago palm, or cycad) of the Myōkoku-ji is the subject of a well-loved Sakai legend, told here in full: Nobunaga coveted the great old plant and had it moved to Azuchi, whereupon it wailed each night to be taken home, until he gave up and returned it. The cycad is not native to Japan; it was carried up from the south, which is why Goemon feels in it a homesickness from far away.
The jō is ten shaku, roughly three metres (for the smaller units of length see chapter 1). The tree thus stood something over three and a half metres, and better than five around at the root.

This ninja explanation of Takeda Shingen’s death belongs to the world of the earlier novel, not to the record. Shingen died in 1573 during the withdrawal from Noda castle; the histories put it down to illness, though one old tradition has it he was hit by a sniper’s ball at the siege. The tale of an Iga poisoner is the story’s own.

The shichihōde, the “seven ways out,” were the seven stock disguises of the Iga and Kōga shinobi for travel in hostile provinces: priest, mountain ascetic, flute-playing komusō, street conjuror, sarugaku player, merchant, and plain townsman. The point, as the ferryman anecdote makes plain, was not costume but total impersonation.

A koku was reckoned as the rice a man eats in a year (about 180 litres), and a warrior’s stipend was measured in it. Thirty koku with three men’s keep is a very small holding — set beside the five hundred thousand koku of a great lord like Mitsuhide, later in the chapter, it marks Goemon’s deliberately humble footing in the Tokugawa house.

ch02.anchor: swift as the wind, still as the forest
ch02.note: The motto of Takeda Shingen’s war-banner, the celebrated Fūrinkazan (“Wind, Forest, Fire, Mountain”), taken from Sun Tzu: swift as wind, silent as forest, fierce as fire, unshakable as mountain. Tradition holds the characters were brushed by Kaisen, the abbot of Erin-ji, whose burning by Nobunaga is the scene here (Kaisen and Erin-ji: see chapter 1).

The old war-tales made much of Nobunaga humiliating Akechi Mitsuhide — the beating before the gate of Erin-ji, the stripping of the banquet office at Azuchi — and treated these slights as the spur to the Honnō-ji revolt three weeks later. Modern historians read most of it as later embroidery and leave Mitsuhide’s true motive an open question; the novel adopts the traditional, dramatic account, and adds a hidden hand behind it.

ch02.anchor: Momochi Sandayū and Fujibayashi Nagato-no-kami had been one and the same man
ch02.note: The notion that Iga’s two legendary chief shinobi were a single man wearing two names comes out of the earlier novel (on the pair, see chapter 1). Goemon guards the secret because he alone is placed to know it, and because it cannot, he thinks, be disproved.

Nobunaga’s best-loved page and, by tradition, his boy-lover; such bonds (nanshoku) between a lord and a youth were an accepted part of samurai life. Ranmaru and his younger brothers Bōmaru and Rikimaru all died at his side at the Honnō-ji. He was about eighteen.

ch02.anchor: The enemy is at the Honnō-ji.
ch02.note: The most famous line of the whole affair, put in Mitsuhide’s mouth as he turned his army from the Bitchū road toward Kyoto. It is almost certainly a later dramatist’s invention rather than a recorded utterance, but it has become the shorthand for the betrayal itself (on the Honnō-ji: see chapter 1).

ch02.anchor: At Mount Hiei you burned a thousand six hundred souls
ch02.note: Goemon’s indictment lists Nobunaga’s notorious slaughters: the burning of the Tendai monastery on Mount Hiei in 1571 (Mount Hiei: see chapter 1), and the massacre of the Ikkō leagues penned up at Nagashima in Ise in 1574, where tens of thousands were burned to death — figures vary widely, and the fourteen thousand given here is at the low end of the estimates.

ch02.anchor: the perils of the Iga crossing
ch02.note: Ieyasu’s flight home after the Honnō-ji Incident, over the mountains of Iga to his own country, guided by Hattori Hanzō’s Iga men — the celebrated “Iga crossing” (the same escape called the Tarao Crossing in chapter 1), long remembered as the tightest scrape of his life.

The Peanuts were Emi and Yumi Itō, identical-twin sisters and one of the most popular singing acts in the Japan of the early 1960s, when this novel was being written — and, to Western readers, the tiny twin fairies of the Mothra films. The author reaches into his own present for a resemblance no reader of his day could miss.

The author, Murayama Tomoyoshi (1901–1977) — avant-garde painter, playwright, and director of the proletarian theatre — was repeatedly tailed and jailed for his left-wing work in the 1930s. His running asides on detectives and their memory for faces, like the tirade earlier in the chapter, come straight out of that experience (compare the aside on the Special Higher Police in chapter 1).

En no Gyōja (En no Ozunu), the semi-legendary seventh-century ascetic revered as the founder of Shugendō, the mountain asceticism that the novel treats as the root of ninjutsu. The Peacock King (Kujaku Myōō) whose rite follows is a wisdom-king invoked in esoteric Shingon against poison and sickness and for long life.

ch02.anchor: Kōbō Daishi, founder of the Shingon sect
ch02.note: Kūkai (774–835), the great master of esoteric Buddhism. Believers hold that he did not die but sits in eternal meditation in the inner sanctuary (Oku-no-in) of Kōya-san, awaiting the future Buddha Maitreya — who is said to come five and a half billion years after Śākyamuni — and that the pilgrim who nears his tomb, chanting “Namu Daishi Henjō Kongō,” draws near a living presence. The narrator sets this beside the Christian hope of the Second Coming.

The author, a lifelong Marxist, quietly enlists his outlaw hero in his own creed: death is the end, the soul only a working of the body. The “us” is the tell — the whole long meditation on resurrection and deathlessness is the materialist author measuring the consolations of religion and finding them wanting, while granting how naturally the people of Goemon’s age lived inside them.
